strings.BAH_Mobsters_Paradise_desc:
The late 50s were a time of crisis for American organized crime as the one-two punch of Kefauver's crackdown and Castro's revolution left the mafia reeling. Casinos and brothels from Vegas to Havana were shuttered, and great empires of sin were reduced to dust. But all was not lost, for a new promised land awaited those fortunate or cunning enough to escape Johnny Law: the Bahamas.

Nassau, a haven for ne'er-do-wells since the Golden Age of Piracy, was the perfect locale for the mafia diaspora to make their new home. The Bay Street oligarchs who ran the joint were more than willing to let their new partners in crime get back on their feet in exchange for some obligatory graft. Casinos, brothels, and drug dens blot the land as her new residents labor to create a paradise of debauchery to rival Sodom and Gomorrah.
strings.BAH_Rule_Bay_Street_desc: A remnant of colonial-era society, the progeny of white political dynasties have formed a ruling class known as the Bay Street Boys. Unofficially, they have created a network of elites to control every facet of national affairs by proxy via the puppet United Bahamian Party. Exercising almost unlimited power over the islands through gerrymandering and other illicit means, they are currently most interested in maintaining white rule and filling their coffers by any means.
strings.BAH_Sandcastle_desc: Since Stafford Sands' visionary tenure as the Minister of Finance began, the Bahamas has transitioned into an unofficial policy of unfettered “free-range” capitalism to foster its burgeoning tourism and gambling industries. As the coffers of the central government and her collaborators steadily grow, the shifting sands of the islands continue to bury the citizenry under festering corruption and poverty.
strings.BAH_Closing_Bay_Street_desc:
With the UBP dissolved and the Bay Street Boys a historical footnote, the Bahamians have, for the first time throughout their history, found themselves ruled under a semblance of real democracy.

Although the new majority rule remains imperfect as the white elites continue to hold disproportionate influence, the ruling PLP has nonetheless been able to maintain a strong public opinion. However, with a charismatic yet overbearing leadership dominating over every aspect of the party, some fear that the Bahamas will soon fall under another uniparty system.
strings.BAH_Knocking_Sandcastle_desc: The Bahamas are presently dominated by the interests of tourists and financial moguls, and Lynden Pindling now works tirelessly to reign in the unregulated green line nightmare Stafford Sands created—his goal is to redistribute the profit for the people's broad benefit. Of course, this effort has already brought conflict with those few who until now have reaped the nation's bounty. If he seeks to see these reforms through, the barons will not go gently.
strings.BAH_Repaving_Bay_Street_desc: The Bay Street oligarchy in Nassau, long dominated by white elites who have thus controlled the islands' economy, has shown a willingness towards reform, including a larger role for black up-and-comers. However, while it's clear that the old, white plutocrats run the show from the shadows even now, what isn't clear is how long this situation can stand. How strong are the winds of change?
strings.BAH_Mafia_Cooperate_tt: We will work towards coopting the Bahamian Mafia.
strings.BAH_Mafia_Burn_tt: We will work towards eliminating the Mafia from Bahamas.
strings.BAH_forpol.1.desc:
Vincent Teresa's suite on the top floor of the Flamingo Hotel only sought to affirm its reputation. Filled with every amenity and constantly inhabited by a mixture of informants, mafia members and hotel staff, it overlooked the back half of Paradise Island. Sitting above the bridge to Nassau and the heart of the Bahamas, it came as the height of luxury. As a new band of cleaners left the room, knowing better than to intervene in mob affairs, a fresh band of informants waltzed in.

“This doesn't come cheap, you know,” murmured Teresa, so casual as to almost become inaudible, rolling a burning cigar in his hand as he looked down at the streets below him, awash with people featureless beyond their presence. “I'm a wealthy man, but even my money has its limits.”

“And our associates' accounts are even deeper,” replied one, almost rehearsed in its diplomatic tact. “Trust me, Vincent, you're an esteemed guest, and none of us want anything other than the best for you. But our boss expects something in return.”

“I presumed as much,” responded Teresa, chuckling to himself. “What do you want? Looking for a hit on somebody?”

“He wants to expand into the Caribbean, but he's been butting up against some people from here,” replied another, a false Italian twang stretching almost too far to be believed. “I'm no man to bite the hands that feed, but this very hotel is a real headache for us. You'll have to tell us who Bugsy Siegel really works for.”

Teresa pondered the issue for one moment, drawing from his cigar once more, before giving in. “Alright, fine, I'll talk. When he was shut down in Vegas, he didn't just rebuild his casino here for fun. The man's got a deal with Symonette.” Most agents remained silent, waiting for him to continue. “If I do more than talk, I'll be sticking my head out. But with the right deal, I'll prove it.”
strings.BAH_forpol.1.a: Time to make an offer he can't refuse.
strings.BAH_forpol.2.desc:
It had been a long day for Percy Dunn. He had been expecting the report on the mafia's ties to Symonette to be given for a while. What he had instead received was a much larger report, superficially explaining that before then highlighting their ties to fascists across Latin America, and to the Iberian Union.

“Virtually every name is here. Symonette...Duvalier...Batista...Stroessner...you'd be hard pressed to find a fascist not involved in Latin America,” he continued to Theodore Allan absentmindedly. “The ties we have to figures in Florida would be concerning enough; but this? This goes so much further than we expected.” Finally looking up, he grinned slightly.

“So, what do we do about this?” asked Theodore Allan, himself deep in a page about deals between a state representative from Louisiana and an Iberian diplomat.

“Well, we have to convince the government to publish these findings. Failing that, find some journalist. We've redacted enough for our mafia informants to keep the important ones safe, but the magnitude of this report is too great to just leave in an archive.”

Allan shook his head. “Look, none of this is good. We need to get the Iberians out of the Caribbean, and any compromised American asset away from any sphere of influence.” He dropped the report, and leant back into his chair. “Yet if we just reveal it, we'll lose any leverage we have when the Bahamian government collapses. Besides, the Iberian government is bad, but would you rather Japan get their tendrils there instead?

Dunn looked with some scepticism, but shrugged his shoulders. ”I can get your worry. It's not our choice, anyway.“ Opening a flask, he poured a glass of whiskey before leaving it to simmer in his hand for a moment. ”Whatever we want, it's the FBI Director's choice.“
strings.BAH_forpol.2.a: We can't tolerate this. Seek out the American government; this must be made public.
strings.BAH_forpol.2.b: This has more use as blackmail than a headline. The threat should get the Bahamas back in line.
strings.BAH_forpol.3.desc:
Around a roulette table, empty laughter bellowed loud enough to echo across rooms. A small group had emerged: a trio of local American mobsters brought over to the Bahamas by Bugsy Siegel, an Iberian businessman looking to expand his business with likeminded gentlemen, and a croupier who waxed polemic about the fall of nearby lands to communism. They joked, laughed and relaxed into each other's company, but they all knew it was a lie.

“You ever kill a man?” asked one, Albert, as conversation picked up around them. The Iberian businessman looked ahead with mild confusion, before indicating that he continued as the ball landed on 36 Red.

Albert bet on black as the Iberian stuck to red, and then momentarily pondered his next move. “Yeah, we've all killed a few. We had this one guy, big name in Newark, but couldn't keep his mouth shut 'round coppers. So we took him out to the woods. Told him we were taking a hit out on another rat. And then, when he shot the guy, I shot him as well. Two birds with one stone, gone.”

13 Black. The Iberian grimaced, both at the loss and at his strategy. “Pretty risky strategy, no?” asked Alfonso, as he called a large bet on Red.

Albert shrugged, before his group moved forwards most of their stakes. “I'm a guy who likes taking risks.”

Alfonso smiled, placing forth a similar bet. “I was too young to fight against the Bolsheviks or to take back Gibraltar, but I was old enough to trick the army into thinking I was old enough in 1944. I was stationed outside of Bamako when a sandstorm came in. Unlike most people, I took the risk.” The ball lingered for a moment, before stopping at 2 Red, drawing an angry eye from the mobsters. “Three fewer American troops walking those streets today, let me say.”
strings.BAH_forpol.3.a: Alfonso then placed his largest bet yet.
strings.BAH_forpol.3.b: Memories of a war once fought, and warnings of the war yet to be fought.
strings.BAH_forpol.4.desc:
The relative wealth of the streets around Madrid drew Armando Gaona's attention, but only superficially. He never needed to feel that shared wealth to take in his own splendour. None of his group did. But times were changing; with the Caribbean Legion now in control of the Dominican Republic, he and his group of Trujillist businessmen had to find a new place to go. Madrid was just a provisional stop booked at the last minute.

“It was a real shame to see Rafael Trujillo fall, you know,” grumbled Joaquín Carballar, lighting a cigar. “Never knew the man myself, but he was the perfect man to help my business expand over there.”

“Yeah, it was. Few men were ever as big a help as us,” replied Maximiliano Illescas, spewing from a cigar in turn. “Madrid is a nice city, but we still have business in the Caribbean. Any places you'd recommend?”

Carballar thought for a second, and then leant into Illescas' ear, still speaking loud enough to be heard by all. “If you're willing to take a less...conventional route, then try the Bahamas. For the right price, you can get anything.” He tapped his nose, before leaning back.

The group murmured, intrigued by the suggestion, but their responses took on a more hesitant tone. “I'm sure you can, Joaquín, but will he be accommodating to us?” asked Armando. “He's an American, and we wouldn't be talking about this if America had stayed away.”

Armando tried to continue, but was hushed by Joaquín as he spoke. “Symonette doesn't care about America. As long as you help to bring business into Nassau and keep those lawless savages he lives with down, he won't care if you're Franco or Salazar.” Murmuring repeated itself once more, hesitance now replaced by nodding and interest.
strings.BAH_forpol.4.a: The next country on an ignominious list.
strings.BAH_forpol.5.desc:
From the moment Vincent Teresa had started talking, he knew it was only a matter of time until his associates caught on. He noticed it everywhere; he could see it in his handshakes with other mobsters, he could feel it in their glares. Yet he could not help but hold onto hope. Just cutting himself off from other mobsters would only raise suspicion, and so, he tried to pretend that nothing had happened. Only when his latest frenetic jabberings had stopped did he realise just how far out to sea his yacht had become.

“Alright, let's stop playing around like this,” sighed one as he raised his gun, a motion almost instantly echoed by the rest of the yacht.

He knew it. Might as well fight the inevitable, he thought. “Woah, what are you doing?” exclaimed Teresa, taking one step backwards.

“We know what you've been doing, Vince,” replied the first man, barely moving as he raised his gun. “We've been told what you've been doing by the boss. The Spanish are telling me you've been ratting their friends out to the feds. Awful thing to bite the hands feeding you.”

“What? I would never!” responded Teresa, feigning shock. Suddenly, the realisation had come to him. He'd been conned. “Come on, I'd never do that, believe me. Hey, let's not mess ar-”

-BANG-

Pain seared through Teresa's chest, paralysing him in shock. He stumbled back, one step, then two, before the second man lowered his gun and pushed him off. They lingered for a moment more, watching the blood red fade into a murkier blue, before the shapes drove off, their grumbles about the upcoming loss of such a good boat obscured beneath waves and a fading consciousness.
strings.BAH_forpol.5.a: The sea's hunger is sated once more.
strings.BAH_forpol.6.desc:
They should've known not to wait too long. From the moment their agents in the Bahamas had suddenly gone silent, they should've known that something was up with their connection to Vincent Teresa. By the time the FBI had realised, Teresa's yacht was long gone from harbour. His reservations at the Flamingo Hotel had been totally emptied and new adverts for his exclusive suite had been plastered over newspapers. A clandestine group of agents slowly gathered, preparing to account for the worst.

The room had been totally ransacked, the only sign of care being an initially locked door and a carefully shuttered set of curtains. Virtually everything else was upturned, spilt, or missing. As they flicked through the cabinets and drawers, any evidence of the files they had once seen were totally gone, with only a single manila folder that had fluttered beneath the bed and a pair of empty clothes hangers being evidence that anything beyond a tsunami had ever been present in the room.

What had happened was clear. Vincent Teresa, at some stage, had acted suspicious, and the FBI had prepared too slowly. Iberian agents had doubtlessly organised his disappearance, probably throwing him off of his yacht to drown, before then moving on. They waited in the room for a moment, waiting to see if any other staff members would come, hoping to see if they could explain something. Nobody arrived. For now, the staff were smart enough not to intervene in mob affairs.

Defeated, they slinked out of the ransacked suite, complaining about missed opportunities in hesitant whispers. They knew something was afoot, but now they had no solid leads. If the other informants hadn't already been purged, Teresa's death would give them too much cause. Their leads on Symonette's ties to Iberia or the Mafia were completely gone. As they limped down the stairs, their gazes shifted to his empty table at the casino. And so, their minds turned to an evening of gambling.
strings.BAH_forpol.6.a: And as evening turned to night, the agents bet all of their winnings on black.
strings.BAH_forpol.7.desc:
Roland Symonette reclined in his chair, studying Kendal Isaacs, a black member of the UBP, and his handpicked successor, to discuss the transition to majority rule for the nation.

“At this rate, Kendal,” Symonette began, voice low and weary in a way that felt more practiced than sincere. “The people want majority rule, and they want a face that reflects it. An old white man like me at the helm... well, it's no longer tenable. So, as a compromise, I'll step back from the forefront and let you take the premiership.”

Isaacs leaned forward in his chair. “Well, thank you for your service, Symonette-”

Symonette cut him off with a limp wave. “My service is not finished. Don't misunderstand. I may be leaving the public eye of the premiership, but I will still be... let's say, guiding matters, giving advice. Just making sure the country stays on its present course.” Leaning forward, voice sharpening. “Stability is essential. You'll need my hand on certain matters, even if the populace sees yours.”

A flicker of irritation crossed Isaacs's face before he smothered it. He had known this was coming. “Of course,” Isaacs said, forcing a polite smile. “I'll keep you informed.” Isaacs knew he needed Symonette's graces if he wished to lead the UBP.
strings.BAH_forpol.7.a: Even if it meant bowing for now.
strings.BAH_forpol.8.t: A Loose Leash Is Still a Leash
strings.BAH_forpol.8.desc:
The conference hall was filled with a buzz of diplomats and elites, flags of the West Indies Federation hung in adjacent with those of the Bahamas. Kendal Isaacs meticulously looked over the details of his speech; this was his moment of history. His moment to put the Bahamas on his path. Behind him stood Roland Symonette, a man without position, yet he was able to strongarm his way here. Shaking hands with old friends and foreign dignitaries from across the Caribbean, taking every photo and every deal that he could. Although joining the Federation wasn't something he'd have done in office, he allowed Isaacs to pursue the idea.

“Roland,” Isaacs murmured under his breath, “I thought you said you'd keep a low profile.”

Symonette didn't bother hiding his amusement. “And I will. But let's not pretend the Bahamas has something to gain from these eager diplomats. Best to get as much as I can before it ends.” Before Isaacs could respond, another influential Anglophile strode over, beaming at Symonette.

“Roland, old chap! I heard you'd stepped back, but here you are, still keeping the ship steady.”

Symonette accepted the compliment with a gracious nod. “Merely offering guidance where needed. Kendal, here is the future, of course.”

Isaacs stood beside them, smiling thinly, feeling the ground shift beneath him. Every time he tried to interject, the Anglophile's attention slid back to Symonette. Every agreement Symonette hinted at, however unofficial, made Isaacs's task harder. He needed the Bahamas to appear sovereign, confident, and fully committed to the Federation. Instead, Symonette's shadow loomed over every conversation. And sooner or later, he would have to step out of Symonette's shadow.
strings.BAH_forpol.8.a: Whether Symonette allowed it or not.
strings.BAH_forpol.10.desc:
Darnell Fox looked over his shoulder and licked his lips nervously. Was the person he had seen a block ago another passerby or a tail? Had he seen that car before on another street? He was in a safehouse, a dingy nondescript building in a poor neighborhood on the outskirts of Nassau, but was it truly safe? Everything seemed normal, but if he was being followed by a pro, then he wouldn't know that he was being followed, would he? He dialed a long stream of numbers to contact his American contact, Freeman.

The Bay Street Boys were the ruling clique on the islands, and while everyone knew that they washed money for the American syndicates and took in guns from other murderous Latin American strongmen, it was one thing to know, and another thing to have proof. If there was any hope of a Bahamian People's Republic, then the people needed to know that the Bay Street Boys were killing their people at the behest of the Americans, and the American public needed to know that their precious leaders were letting criminals run rampant over the natives. In the States, there were people talking about the right for the Black Man to stand up for himself, to achieve everything that life had to offer, not whatever scraps the White Man saw fit to toss his way. He heard the phone crackle with connection

Darnell believed in the cause when he had volunteered to surveil the Bay Street Boys's warehouse in Prince George port. Even now, his heart welling up in his throat, he still believed. The faith in the cause is what gave him the strength to even imagine standing up to the Bay Street Boys. When he delivered his observations, that faith would spread across the islands and beyond, and finally place the Bahamas in the hands of people like him. A state for people who looked like him.

Darnell only felt a slight touch from a cold barrel before the bullet shattered his skull. All he had seen and heard; now, he would never do either ever again because of what he hadn't.
strings.BAH_forpol.10.a: Freeman dropped the handset in utter shock, his heart gripped in his chest, and, fearful, looked over his own shoulder.
strings.BAH_forpol.11.desc:
“Well, the beaches around Florida were a wonderful place to grow up. Really acclimatises you to this place,” mused Roland Symonette, idly looking at his glass of wine. Ezequiel de Sousa nodded along, growing tired of pleasantries. Iberia had sought a discreet route of exports to Jamaica, and knew better than to take Symonette's claims of reform seriously.

“I have happy memories from my own childhood, Roland, but we can do better than reminisce,” replied de Sousa, struggling to conceal his accent. “Let's talk business.”

Symonette's eyes returned to de Sousa, but his tone remained flat. “Of course. A small island chain like mine can't survive without business. What kind of venture were you proposing?”

De Sousa struggled to broach the topic. “Well, we wanted to ship some goods through Freeport down to Jamaica, but it must be discreet.”

“Trade is important, Ezequiel,” replied Symonette, even flatter than before. “If it wants to prosper, the Caribbean will need it.”

“I won't deny that,” replied de Sousa, struggling not to roll his eyes. “If we can come to a deal, I can assure you that Iberian ships will happily pass through your ports.”

Symonette turned back to his glass, spinning the liquid inside around, before taking a lengthy sip. “I welcome the idea of doing business with all nations, and it would be nice to see more Iberians with us.” He wanted more.

“Alright, Roland, how much money do you want!?” snapped De Souza, tired of the exchanges. For a moment, he held his breath, worrying that his lack of decorum had broken the deal, but Symonette's arms suddenly broadened.
strings.BAH_forpol.11.a: “Glad we can do business together, Ezequiel.”
strings.BAH_forpol.12.desc:
From the stories he eavesdropped on outside bars. From the squawks of seagulls flying overhead. From the tiniest of slits between the hotel gates. Ajani had only known the beach from Nassau's dankest alleyways, a beach littered with wealth and cocktails that only welcomed white tourists.

But today, only a sign declaring “PRIVATE PROPERTY” stopped Ajani from occupying the sandy waterfront.

Ajani was the first to step past the invisible line in the sand. A wall to separate white and black folks like himself. He was twelve. Not much younger than the folks in America who would do sit-ins at bars. The others followed. Cousins, classmates, and cricket teammates he'd play with on the weekends. The ocean's ebbs hissed as it scratched at the sands.

“Off the sand!” A man roared. Two more followed behind him, holding a nailed bat and a crowbar. “Your kind can't read the damn sign?”

Some scrambled away. But Ajani met the man's gaze. He dug his soles in the sand. The sand reciprocated, giving way to his ankles and rooting him safely. A boy shouted back. “We can read alri-”

A baton slammed into the boy's jaw.

Ajani didn't remember deciding to move. He only remembered the sands pushing him forward. He only remembered his fist connecting. He only remembered ripping the crowbar out of one of their hands and swinging it blindly.

But the boys remained on the dunes. The red had already been washed away, creating a murky purple in the waters. Ajani looked down at his hands. They shook. The sign still stood at the edge of the beach. Ajani walked up to it, crowbar in hand.
strings.BAH_forpol.12.a: And with one swing, he knocked down the first wall.
strings.BAH_forpol.13.desc:
Shoving a filled suitcase shut and shunting it to the side, Roland Symonette looked around frantically, trying to find another one. Money this time, of course, most possessions worth keeping had been sent off long ago. Most of his familiar places had long since been emptied, but as he sifted through the bedsheets and floorboards, loose notes still came out. For a moment, Symonette allowed himself time for pause, looking outside at Nassau. The streets were empty, but he knew that most were simply inside, celebrating with family.

Not that he had ever wanted to join them, of course. As soon as the Bahama Papers had been released, he'd been totally abandoned. Iberian diplomats had been unceremoniously dumped, mafia members had been arrested, American representatives had resigned. All for show, of course. He knew how deep his ties had run previously, but that didn't matter in the face of public outrage. With Pindling's landslide, his ship had finally crashed; no use staying in the country now.

Symonette rummaged through his drawers one last time, grabbing suits for wads of cash and cramming them into another suitcase. He could feel the glares of his Bahamian staff, but cared not to answer them. No matter their silence, he knew how they had voted, and knew he would never see them again past today. Whisking his hand, he ordered an entering employee to bring it down, and then took a deep breath. Nothing was left beyond walls, empty cabinets and an unmade bed.

In turn, he shut off the light, and rushed out of the building. The Learjet behind him was still being filled with luggage, but was otherwise primed to take flight. Not everybody had abandoned him, thankfully; an American businessman was more than happy to allow him access to a spare home until the press surrounding him had died down. As he clambered up the stairs, he took a final moment to take in the warm air surrounding him, before leaving as he watched a pair of fresh cars arrive.
strings.BAH_forpol.13.a: One last crime before surrendering the spotlight.
strings.BAH_forpol.14.desc:
The soft glow of sunset washed through the windows of the Grande Cove Casino, tinting the rooms within a burning orange from the seas of the Exuma Sound. Few lights were on; even fewer people complained. A stream of guests had gambled away, but their numbers were thinning, and nobody was replacing them. Overlooking the crowd, in a private suite, the trio of American businessmen who owned the casino silently commiserated on their upcoming loss.

“Well, the bastard's going through with it,” grumbled Archie Miller, cleaning his spectacles. “Pindling's going to nationalize the place, and maybe give us a boat out of the Bahamas.”

“A paddleboat, maybe,” complained Kenneth O'Neil, stabbing his fork at his plate. “You can see how a fool like him got elected by this lot.” He waved his hand widely, pointing only vaguely to a waitress walking down the aisle. “Too lazy to wait for anything but handouts!”

Miller nodded. “We would've never had this problem with Symonette still in power. He would've sorted it out in a second for a few thousand bucks.”

Clarence Blankenship looked at the empty aisles in front of him, watching a crowd that had slowly dwindled into a pair exchange their final hands, and sighed. “You know, maybe it's for the best. Now that Pindling's in charge, these workers are shiftless. They think the country's theirs - I've even heard them laugh about forming a union.” Eyebrows raised around him as he shook his head. “These natives always plot to rob you behind your backs, let me tell you.”

O'Neil's face became muddled, but he sighed. “Maybe you're right. I don't like it, but perhaps all things have their ends.” He turned to his wine, drinking deeply and swallowing hard. “It's not like Pindling was being fair with his tax demands, anyway.”
strings.BAH_forpol.15.desc:
“You know, it may have moved off of your pages once the Bahama Papers hit, but there's a lot more to say about that story in the Bahamas than came forth,” said Donald Calegari, slicing into his plate of pizza. He had reached out to the New York Times with the promise of a newspaper, but even as he sat in a restaurant owned by a close friend in Brooklyn, he didn't want to wait until dessert.

“What more is there to say?” asked Alexander Hinton, drawing his knife through the crust in front of him. “Symonette worked with a bunch of fascists, several people got arrested and he lost in a landslide. Nobody's interested in rereading old news.”

As Hinton finished, Calegiri heartily laughed. “You really think it ends with Symonette? I've been doing some digging of my own, and Pindling's even worse. Since he nationalized the place, he's been giving contracts to the most corrupt men in the Caribbean.” He brought out a large wad of documents, barely sorted into a number of folders.

“There's a saying, Donald, about throwing stones in glass houses,” responded Joe Leon, through a mouthful of parmesan cheese. “For a laundromat, you sure have dirty hands. You've been arrested for blatant corruption. I have a friend in the police department talking about another investigation.”

Hinton nodded. “Nobody's ever been able to stick you with them yet, but everyone can see your ties to the mafia. We know they've been angry since they lost the Bahamas; why should we trust you?”

“Hey, I'm not asking for glory,” shrugged Calegari, pushing himself back from his chair as he rummaged through his black coat. “You've seen my record. You know I've already gotten mine.” He threw an envelope onto the table, bulging with notes and rubber bands, as he walked away. “Just say it's from an anonymous source.”
strings.BAH_forpol.16.desc:
When he was sent to the Bahamas, the Iberian agent had been told who to expect and where to meet him. Vincent Centanni had been described to him as a gregarious man, his formal suits contrasted with a constant humour and a wide smile. Looking down at the image, he saw that his old visage had long since evaporated. Alone on a stool in a casino with little business, Centanni looked shrunken and sullen, his hair unkempt and his blazer practically hanging off his shoulders.

“Centanni?” A brief look upwards was all that was needed to confirm his apparent downfall. “Madrid sent me. We're getting troubling news regarding our deal with shipments to Jamaica.”

The words barely seemed to get through to Centanni, but he nodded regardless. “A lot of big names were arrested recently,” said Rabellini, looking through his list. “Sergi, Roibén, Emilio, Micolau... these were good agents, Omero. What happened?”

“Look, whatever your name is, this isn't a good time. We don't know who, but somebody's been ratting us out. Direct line to the FBI, and they likely know it. It's probably a big name too, with how many people are getting hit.”

His brow furrowed. “That is concerning. Any idea who the rat is?”

“No, and we won't be finding out soon. If we intervene, the Americans will just arrest everyone involved. If we try finding the rat ourselves, we'll end up killing ourselves in a fit of paranoia.” Centanni took out a cigarette, desperately fiddling with the lighter as he placed it in his mouth. “If you want to keep throwing men into American prisons, be my guest, but the mafia's not in the place to protect your ships anymore.
strings.BAH_forpol.16.a: The agent's brow furrowed, mourning the lost profits.
strings.BAH_forpol.17.desc:
11:22 - Bahamian police given brief on strategy, significant equipment and locations of key smugglers. Presence of direct FBI agents minimal, but Bahamian police seem invested in raid despite conscription.

17:55 - Protests in Jamaica over repressive policy of Alexander Bustamante begin to rise in intensity. Attention of those within Jamaica, including smugglers, should be overstretched by this point. Raids to begin from this point forwards.

18:21 - First major anti-smuggler raid in Montego Bay. Large supply of illicit substances, especially cocaine. Twelve smugglers arrested, two killed in fighting. Significant cache of weaponry discovered and taken in.

19:10 - Second and third major anti-smuggler raids occur, targeting depots outside Mandeville and Ocho Rios.

Few supplies found in either case and only five people arrested, but high number of vehicles captured. Two smugglers escaped, but were quickly killed in a shootout.

21:42 - Fourth major anti-smuggler raid, targeting cell in Blue Mountains closest to Kingston. Seems to have been the heart of the operation, with fifty arrests. High proportion of presumed Iberian agents, who have been forwarded to regular channels, and large numbers of weapons and supplies seized.

23:39 - Last major anti-smuggler operation in Dry Harbour Mountains. Smaller presence, but had most organised defence, killing three before being captured. Limited supplies, but had high quantity of dollars; was likely informed of earlier raids.

23:40-01:00 - Cleanup operations, focused on incarcerating those targeted, removing the Bahamian police from Jamaica and constructing press release. Select individuals likely free, but not enough to sustain ring.
strings.BAH_forpol.18.desc:
When he had first gotten the call, John Ramsey's ears picked up at what they implied. Any journalist worth the articles they write would've been intrigued by what the press release alone indicated; the American government had found a hidden network tying Latin American fascists and mobsters to the Iberian Union, tied together by the Bahamas? The promise, and capacity to access, the full papers only drew his attention further. Ramsay was sure that there was more to this story than the thick tomes alone.

Pouring through, his interest only grew further. Press releases smoothed out any concerns and replaced them with harsh condemnations of Franco and Symonette, but beneath it, the real gravity of the Bahama Papers were clear. American officials and American politicians were clearly shown as being happy to collaborate with fascists and the mafia where there was a profit to be made. The ties between some of the Senators listed alone would be enough to fill headlines for a full week the nation over.

Or so he thought. As soon as he tried to extend his reporting beyond the small cast President {usa_getleader} had recited, he found his reports shut down. It wasn't their field, they claimed, or the reporting had too little meat to it to genuinely be published, or that it was a crypto-Japanese plot, or was tabloid-level, or that they couldn't pay the subsequent legal fees to defend from claims of libel. No matter how he tried to appeal, no matter who he talked to, nobody would listen.

A few days later, Ramsey reached out to the Village Voice. His offering and background was unconventional, and he found himself uncomfortable at just how left-wing the paper was, but he saw it as better than nothing, and was assured that his own writing would be largely unaffected by the crowd. Within the day, news of the story broke across telephone lines and networks, and within the week, the story was front page news across countercultural newspapers the country over.
strings.BAH_forpol.18.a: But to the reading public, the headline had long since faded.
strings.BAH_forpol.19.desc:
Warm air bucketed Theodore Allan as he marched through the lobby of the Flamingo Hotel. Its shine felt a world removed from the dirt roads he had been driven through after reaching the Bahamas, but it sank away as he threw Siegel's door open. After a cry of protest over his interruption, Allan quickly turned to speak.

“Bugsy Siegel, I'm with the FBI. I know you've been smuggling goods into Jamaica alongside Iberia.” Allan slammed a document down. “Emilio Escribano. Micolau Vicedo. Davi-”

“I work with a lot of guys.” Siegel kept a cool face, but a hint of concern betrayed him. “I'm a businessman. What do you want me to say?”

Allan raised a file. “I could take this to the FBI Director and have him leak the whole thing. The Nevada police were pissed that we let you go free in the first place, and now this? Treason carries a death sentence, you know. Or, you can talk.”

“Why talk?” asked Siegel, nervously, ordering the door to be shut.

“We'll let you keep all of this. We might even turn a blind eye to what your men have been doing in Queens lately.” Allan leaned in, poking a finger directly into Siegel's chest. “But you'll tell us every last area here that Iberia influences.”

Bugsy Siegel looked downtrodden, sinking into his chair. “By the time I'd get enough information to work with, my associates will know who the rat is, and the-”

“You're dead already, Bugsy. Where would you rather be shot? Your throne or the chair?” Allan pointed to a phone number. “I know what you mobsters are like. You'll give me what I want soon enough.”
strings.BAH_forpol.19.a: A dirty deal done dirt cheap.
strings.BAH_News.1.t: {get_newspaper_header}Majority Rule Achieved in the Bahamas Amidst Scandal
strings.BAH_News.1.desc:
Following a recent scandal involving several Bahamian government officials, Roland Symonette's cabinet has collectively stepped down in disgrace, marking the end of the United Bahamian Party's hegemony and white rule. Corresponding with other decolonization movements in the region, investigations revealed the Symonette family's dealings with the American mafia, which has led to rumors of American pressure playing a key role in the UBP's fall.

Lynden Pindling has been appointed the first Black Prime Minister under popular mandate and vows to build a Bahamas that serves its people. However, the holdovers from the old power base remain a constant obstacle against real reforms through their empire of crimes and vices. It will be an uphill battle to reform an economy entirely intertwined with the old colonial ways.
strings.BAH_News.1.a: The good fight never stops if we are still fighting.
strings.BAH_News.2.t: {get_newspaper_header}White Rule Limps on in the Bahamas
strings.BAH_News.2.desc:
Against the Free World's pressure and her own people's cries of protest, the Bahamas remains unrepentant in its commitment to white rule as the latest election brings another scion of the Symonette dynasty, Robert “Bobby” Symonette, to the seat of Prime Minister. Known for his connections to crime syndicates as well as maintaining a litany of misconduct accusations, the late Roland Symonette's yacht-loving son has been called out by dissidents lately as a “mafioso unfit for governance.”

Following Symonette's inauguration in the ministerial position, commentators have also noted the family's continued collaboration with the Bahamas' long-standing political clique, known as the Bay Street Boys, to be further eroding domestic opinion on the current minority regime. For now, however, the Princeling can sit tight on his throne, carefree as always.
strings.BAH_News.2.a: Who needs popularity when your pops had friends?
strings.BAH_News.3.t: {get_newspaper_header}First Black Prime Minister of the Bahamas
strings.BAH_News.3.desc:
The Bahamas has achieved a historical milestone as the recent election brings “majority rule” to the small state. While the United Bahamian Party remains in power, the state sees its first black Prime Minister, Kendal Isaacs, sidelining the Bay Street Boys oligarchy back into obscurity.

This outcome was driven by the increased US influence in the region following the downfall of British colonial authorities. The UBP's decision to appoint Isaacs as a candidate is reportedly to be a move towards appeasing Washington and distancing itself from the white-minority rule that had characterized the party. Many speculate, although unsubstantiated, that the Bay Street Boys still hold de facto sway over the newly-shuffled cabinet, and Isaacs remains nothing more than a pawn.
strings.BAH_News.3.a: A sunnier day with a brighter face.
strings.BAH_colonial_DEF: the Crown Colony of the Bahamas
